title: OWLEYE: Zero-Shot Graph Anomaly Detection Across Domains
one_liner: A system that detects unusual patterns in networked data from new domains by learning what normal looks like across multiple different graph types, without needing labeled examples of anomalies.
lead: Graph data represents real-world networks: bank transactions flowing between accounts, devices talking to each other, processes depending on one another. Finding the broken edges, fake nodes, or unusual activity in these networks is called anomaly detection. The hard part: graphs from different domains look nothing alike. A bank network has account IDs and dollar amounts; a device network has IP addresses and packet counts. A model trained on one domain fails on another. OWLEYE solves this by learning what normal structure looks like across many domains at once, then catching what does not fit when it sees a new domain it has never trained on.

problem.h2: Why one model cannot work everywhere
paras: Graphs come in wildly different shapes. A financial network tracks money moving between accounts; each edge has a dollar amount and a timestamp. A cybersecurity network tracks device connections; each edge is a packet type and size. A manufacturing network tracks machine dependencies; each edge is a process trigger. The features (what you measure on each edge and node) are completely different — different number of values, different meanings, different ranges.

A naive approach: train one anomaly detector on graphs from a bank, then run it on graphs from a factory. It fails. The model learned what abnormal looks like in financial patterns, not industrial ones. You need to retrain on the factory data — but you might not have labeled anomalies there. A truly useful detector should spot unusual activity in new domains instantly, using patterns learned from other domains.

The real blocker: the model sees feature vectors (just lists of numbers) that come from different domains, and the same number value means totally different things in each domain. A feature value of 100 might be a normal transaction size in finance but an impossible device count in cybersecurity. The model cannot learn what normal looks like when the same number means something different everywhere.

callout.html: OWLEYE aligns all the feature values across domains so they speak the same language, learns what normal structure looks like across all domains, and then detects anomalies in new domains by checking if they fit the learned patterns.

steps.text: Stretch each domain's features so they sit in a common space, preserving what makes each domain unique.
Collect structural patterns (common edge types, node groupings, connection rules) that repeat across all domains.
Each pattern gets a weight; when the model encounters a graph, it decides which patterns to use.
Using the learned patterns and current graph features, predict what each edge and node should look like.
Nodes and edges that deviate far from the reconstruction are anomalies; nodes that fit well are normal.

paras: OWLEYE modifies two things: (1) how features are represented — it remaps raw features from each domain into a shared aligned space before the model ever sees them, and (2) how anomalies are detected — instead of learning a fixed decision rule, it learns a dictionary of normal patterns and flags anything that does not reconstruct well using those patterns.

hidden.h2: Reconstruction error: the signal for what is normal
hidden.name: reconstruction error
paras: Here is the core mechanism: if you learn what normal graphs look like and then try to rebuild an unseen graph using only normal patterns, normal nodes and edges will rebuild well (small error), but anomalies will not (large error). Reconstruction error is the gap between the real values on each node/edge and what the model predicted based on learned patterns. The paper measures this error for every node and edge; nodes with high error are flagged as anomalies.

How the paper uses it: after learning patterns from multiple domains, OWLEYE feeds an unseen graph through the reconstruction module. It predicts what each feature should be based on the patterns it learned. The difference between predicted and actual is the error signal. Large errors mean the node or edge does not fit any learned normal pattern — anomaly. Small errors mean it fits — normal.

heat.caption: Darker means higher reconstruction error. Marked cells are the anomalies the model should catch.

reads.html: Think of reconstruction error as a temperature: normal things run cool (low error), anomalies run hot (high error). A thermometer for abnormality.

The paper learns a multi-domain pattern dictionary via sparse coding; reconstruction error is the residual norm after sparse representation by dictionary atoms. Anomalies are nodes/edges with large residuals.

mechanism.h2: Why learning patterns across domains lets you catch anomalies anywhere
paras: The mechanism has three layers. First, feature alignment: raw features from different domains mean different things, so OWLEYE learns a transformation that maps all features into a shared space. This is not just squishing numbers; it preserves the relationships within each domain while making domains comparable. Example: a bank account balance of 50k and a device packet count of 50k are mapped to the same range, but edges connecting high-value nodes stay high-value in both domains.

Second, pattern learning: OWLEYE trains on graphs from multiple domains and builds a dictionary. Each entry in the dictionary is a pattern (a typical edge type, a frequent connection structure, a normal attribute combination). The model learns which patterns are truly common across domains. A pattern that only appears in one domain is not favored; patterns that show up in finance AND manufacturing AND security get strong weights.

Third, reconstruction: when a new unseen graph arrives, OWLEYE tries to explain every node and edge using only the learned patterns. Normal graphs fit: their structure and attributes match combinations of known patterns. Anomalies do not fit: a node with weird attribute values, an edge connecting things that never connect normally, or a subgraph structure never seen before. The model cannot reconstruct them cleanly, leaving a large error gap. Thresholding that error catches the anomalies.

Why this works across new domains: because the patterns learned across existing domains are general structural rules (like 'normal star-shaped clusters' or 'typical edge attributes range'), not domain-specific ones. A new domain's graph is built from the same kinds of structural building blocks, so the learned patterns apply. Anomalies break these structural rules in any domain; the same error signal works everywhere.

stages.s: Select patterns from dictionary that fit
Reconstruct each node and edge from patterns

math.h2: The reconstruction formula and a worked example
math.words: reconstruction error is the squared difference between the real attribute values on a node and the values you predict using dictionary patterns. Total anomaly score sums errors across all nodes and edges.
symbols: reconstruction error for node or edge i
the real attribute values for node or edge i
the weight (how much we use pattern k)

adding up contributions from all patterns

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose a node has real features [amount=100, time=50]. Pattern dict has two patterns: Pattern A = [amount=90, time=45], Pattern B = [amount=110, time=55].
The model selects alpha_A=0.7, alpha_B=0.3 (favor Pattern A). Prediction = 0.7*[90,45] + 0.3*[110,55] = [63+33, 31.5+16.5] = [96, 48].
Error = (100-96)^2 + (50-48)^2 = 16 + 4 = 20. A small error means the node fits learned patterns.

If a node had real features [amount=200, time=5] (abnormal: big amount, tiny time), neither pattern predicts this well. Prediction stays around [96, 48]. Error = (200-96)^2 + (5-48)^2 = 10816 + 1849 = 12665. Huge error: anomaly flagged.

math.note: The error measures how far the real features sit from what the learned patterns expect, so large errors spot things that break normal structure.

bars.h2: Naïve detector vs. OWLEYE on unseen graph domains

charts.title: Detector trained on domain A only
charts.note: Trained on only one domain, it fails when the features and structure of new domains differ.

charts.title: OWLEYE trained on A + other domains
charts.note: Learning shared patterns across domains transfers to new domains. The gap between A and B/C shrinks because structure is general.

items.html: If you only see graphs from 1 or 2 source domains, the learned patterns are not truly general. They will miss anomalies in a new domain that breaks patterns you never saw. OWLEYE needs diverse domains in training so the patterns cover the full range of normal structures.

items.b: Domains with no clear normal pattern.
items.html: If the source domains are themselves noisy or have no consistent structure, the pattern dictionary will be unreliable. The reconstruction error becomes meaningless because even normal graphs do not reconstruct well.

If an anomaly subtly mimics normal patterns (a fake transaction with all realistic feature values, or a malicious device using typical communication patterns), reconstruction error will be low and it will not be flagged. OWLEYE relies on anomalies being structurally different, not just semantically deceptive.
When you train on multiple diverse domains and anomalies break structural patterns, OWLEYE catches them accurately without any labeled examples from the new domain.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a tiny dataset with three domains: a financial graph (10 nodes, 20 edges with amount and time features), a security graph (10 nodes, 20 edges with packet type and size), and a manufacturing graph (10 nodes, 20 edges with process ID and latency). Inject 2-3 anomalies into each (fake high-value edges, nodes with impossible feature combinations, isolated nodes). Train OWLEYE on the first two domains. Then test on the third domain without retraining. Measure: what fraction of anomalies are caught? What fraction of normal nodes are falsely flagged? For comparison, train a baseline detector on just domain 1, then test on domain 3.
demo.metric_eq: detection rate = anomalies caught / total anomalies injected; false positive rate = normal nodes flagged / total normal nodes
demo.closing: The demo must show OWLEYE catching most anomalies in domain 3 without seeing any labels or retraining, while a single-domain baseline fails.
